title: Cake pops
subtitle: crumbled sponge and buttercream rolled into rounds on sticks
excerpt: Cake pops are formed by crumbling a baked sponge, binding it with a small amount of buttercream, rolling into balls, and coating in tempered chocolate or candy melts. They are a way to use up cake trimmings and the technique is more about proportion and chilling than any particular skill. Too much buttercream and they taste dense and greasy; the right amount makes a compact, fudgy centre.
sourceNotes: Cake pops became a widespread home-baking format in the late 2000s, popularised by US baker Bakerella (Angie Dudley) from 2008 onwards. The technique builds on an older confectionery tradition of chocolate-dipped truffles and rum balls; the lollipop-stick format is the distinguishing element. They were adopted into the UK home-baking repertoire through the early 2010s.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncoated balls on a tray, transfer to a bag once solid. Coat from frozen, adding 2 minutes drying time.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales directly. One batch of standard sponge makes 20 to 24 pops.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Balls can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Coat on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A compound coating chocolate made with vegetable fat instead of cocoa butter. It sets firm at room temperature without tempering, which makes it practical for coating cake pops and dipping items.

content.text: Cake pops are small spheres of crumbled sponge bound with buttercream, set on a lollipop stick, and coated in chocolate or

. The method is simple but proportion matters: bind too tightly and the centre is dense; too loose and the ball falls off the stick. The chill at each stage holds everything together long enough to coat cleanly.

Start with 300 g of completely cooled sponge cake, any flavour. Remove any hard crusts from the base and sides. Break the cake into a large bowl and crumble with your fingers until you have even, fine crumbs, the size of coarse breadcrumbs. No large lumps. The crumbling is easier with day-old or slightly stale cake; freshly baked sponge can become gummy.

Add 2 to 3 tablespoons of buttercream (or cream cheese frosting) to the crumbs. Mix with a fork or your hands until the mixture just holds together when pressed. It should feel like stiff damp sand: it holds a ball without crumbling, but not so wet that it is greasy to the touch. Add buttercream a teaspoon at a time if needed. Over-binding is the most common mistake and the hardest to fix.
Scoop level tablespoons of the mixture and roll between your palms into smooth balls, roughly 3 cm in diameter. Place on a baking-paper-lined tray. Refrigerate for 30 minutes until firm to the touch.

Melt a small amount of chocolate or candy melt (about 50 g) and dip the tip of each lollipop stick 1 cm into the coating. Insert the stick halfway into a chilled ball, then return to the tray. Refrigerate for a further 15 minutes. The small dip of chocolate at the stick tip acts as glue, preventing the ball from slipping off during coating.

Melt 300 g of dark, milk, or white chocolate, or candy melts, in a heatproof bowl over barely simmering water. The bowl must not touch the water. Dark chocolate benefits from tempering (down to 28°C, back up to 31°C) for a glossy, snapping coat; candy melts require no tempering. Dip a pop vertically into the coating, submerging the ball completely, then lift straight out. Hold it horizontally and rotate slowly to let excess drip back into the bowl before standing upright in a block of polystyrene or a pop stand to set.

Sprinkles, coloured sugar, or a contrasting drizzle of melted chocolate all stick while the coating is still wet. Work quickly: the coating sets within 2 to 3 minutes at room temperature. If using candy melts, the coat sets faster than tempered chocolate.

attrs.problem: Ball falls off the stick during coating

content.text: The ball was not cold enough, or the chocolate glue on the stick tip was not set before dipping. Chill the assembled pops for longer before coating, and make sure the stick-tip chocolate is firm.

The ball was too cold when dipped. The temperature difference between a very cold centre and room-temperature coating causes the chocolate to contract and crack as the centre warms. Take the pops out of the fridge 5 minutes before coating.
